title: Ecclesiastical Reform in the Eleventh Century
orientation: This chapter covers the eleventh-century reform movement that transformed the Church from the corrupt, aristocrat-controlled institution of the tenth century into a disciplined, centralized papal monarchy capable of confronting the Empire -- and, at the century's end, produced the first scholastic philosophers, above all Saint Anselm, inventor of the ontological argument for God's existence. It matters because it establishes both the institutional power base from which the medieval Church would police philosophical orthodoxy, and the first genuinely new piece of philosophical argument (as opposed to historical narrative) in Part II.
historical_background: The eleventh century brought Europe's first lasting progress since the fall of Rome: Norman conquerors expelled the Saracens from Sicily and pacified France and England, the Hungarians ceased raiding after conversion, and architecture and education advanced markedly. Reform began with moral concern over corrupt clergy (widespread simony and clerical marriage/'concubinage') but developed an increasingly political dimension: separating clergy from lay control and increasing clerical power. The reform of the papacy was initially driven by the Emperor Henry III, who deposed corrupt and simoniacal popes and installed reformers; but once the papacy had thereby gained moral authority, it turned to assert independence from, and eventually superiority over, the Emperor -- a conflict (Nicholas II's 1059 election decree, the Patarine movement in Milan, and above all Gregory VII's Investiture Controversy with Henry IV, culminating in the humiliation at Canossa in 1077 and Gregory's death in Norman-controlled exile in 1085) that would continue for two centuries.
philosophical_problems: What is the relationship between the Church's economic and institutional interests (control over appointments, revenue, property) and its stated moral and religious motives for reform?
Can the existence of God be proven by reason alone, from the very definition of 'God,' without appeal to revelation or experience? (Anselm's ontological argument)
Is transubstantiation, and more broadly sacramental efficacy, compatible with the personal unworthiness of the priest administering it?
Is God bound by the laws of logic (the law of contradiction), or can He, as Peter Damian argued, do what is logically impossible, including undoing the past?

philosophers_discussed.name: Peter Damian
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Eleventh-century monk and reformer, follower of the hermit Romuald, who reluctantly served as papal legate; author of a treatise On Divine Omnipotence arguing God can act contrary to the law of contradiction and can undo the past (a view later rejected by Aquinas); led the successful anti-simony campaign at Milan in 1059.

philosophers_discussed.name: Berengar of Tours
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A rationalist (d. 1088) who maintained reason is superior to authority, appealing to John the Scot in support; denied transubstantiation and was twice compelled to recant, with his heresies combated by Lanfranc.

philosophers_discussed.name: Lanfranc
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Italian dialectician turned theologian, monk and then prior of Bec in Normandy, who refuted Berengar's denial of transubstantiation in De corpore et sanguine Domini and was made archbishop of Canterbury by William the Conqueror in 1070.

philosophers_discussed.name: Saint Anselm
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Italian monk at Bec (like Lanfranc) and later archbishop of Canterbury (1093-1109); inventor of the 'ontological argument' for God's existence, and otherwise a Platonist and Augustinian who held reason subordinate to faith ('I believe in order to understand').

philosophers_discussed.name: Gerbert (Pope Sylvester II)
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Described as the tenth century's only figure of philosophical note, and even he 'more a mathematician than a philosopher'; quoted satirizing the sale of ecclesiastical office.

philosophers_discussed.name: Gregory VII (Hildebrand)
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The central reforming Pope (1073-1085) who enforced clerical celibacy, initiated the investiture controversy, and clashed with Emperor Henry IV, forcing his penitential submission at Canossa (1077) before ultimately dying in exile under Norman protection after Henry's later triumph.

schools_discussed: The Patarine reform movement in Milan

core_concepts.name: Anselm's ontological argument
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Anselm defines God as 'the greatest possible object of thought.' He then argues that if such an object did not exist, we could think of another object, exactly like it, that did exist -- and that object would be greater, since existing is greater than merely being thought of. So the greatest possible object of thought must exist, since otherwise a still greater one would be conceivable. Therefore God exists.
core_concepts.precise_definition: An a priori proof of God's existence purporting to derive existence from the very concept or definition of God as the greatest conceivable being, without appeal to observation or revelation.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the first purely logical proof of God's existence in Western philosophy and inaugurates a long history of philosophical engagement (both critical and constructive) across many later systems.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Devised by Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, in the late eleventh century.
examples: Anselm's own formulation: 'We define God as the greatest possible object of thought... Therefore God exists.'
objections: Adversely criticized at the time, then forgotten until the later thirteenth century
Rejected by Thomas Aquinas, whose authority has prevailed among theologians ever since
Kant considered that he had 'demolished it once for all'
competing_positions: Aquinas's alternative proofs of God's existence (the unmoved mover, first cause, etc.), which do not rely on deriving existence from a concept
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Revived in amended form by Descartes; Leibniz thought it could be made valid by proving God's possibility; it underlies, in some sense, Hegel's system and reappears in F. H. Bradley's principle 'What may be and must be, is.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: A purely philosophical proof intended to secure a religious conclusion without appeal to revealed authority.

core_concepts.name: Simony and the campaign against it
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Simony -- the buying and selling of ecclesiastical offices -- was rampant in the tenth and early eleventh centuries: kings sold bishoprics, bishops in turn sold lesser preferments. Reformers attacked this not only as sinful but because it made appointment depend on wealth rather than merit, tied bishops to secular rulers who had sold them their offices, and gave newly appointed clergy strong incentive to recoup their investment through worldly rather than spiritual pursuits.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The sale or purchase of ecclesiastical office or sacraments, condemned by eleventh-century reformers as both a moral sin and a structural cause of episcopal subservience to secular power and of clerical worldliness.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: The campaign against simony was inseparable from the political struggle for clerical independence from lay control, since ending the sale of bishoprics by kings directly undercut royal power over Church appointments.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Widespread throughout the tenth and early eleventh centuries; documented by Peter Damian's 1059 discovery that every cleric in Milan, from the archbishop down, was guilty of it.
examples: Gerbert's (Pope Sylvester II's) satirical description of bishops boasting of recouping the gold they paid for office by selling ordinations in turn
Nicholas II's 1059 decree invalidating future ordinations performed by simoniac clergy (not made retroactive, to avoid invalidating most existing ordinations)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Continued to be a central concern of later medieval and Reformation-era Church reform movements.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: ending simony meant ending royal control over episcopal appointments, feeding directly into the investiture conflict.

core_concepts.name: The campaign for clerical celibacy
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Reformers (misleadingly calling married priests' wives 'concubines') sought to enforce celibacy on the secular clergy, most of whom in practice were married in the eleventh century. The moral case (celibacy as a higher spiritual state) was reinforced by practical concerns: married priests tried to pass on Church property to their sons, and a married clergy seemed less separated from, and therefore less able to command reverence from, the laity.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The eleventh-century enforcement of mandatory celibacy on secular (parish) clergy, distinguishing the Western from the Eastern Church (where married parish priests remain permitted), driven by both genuine ascetic conviction and the political-economic goal of preventing hereditary alienation of Church property.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Like the campaign against simony, it served to separate the clergy as a distinct caste from the laity, increasing clerical prestige and institutional cohesion, and was pursued by Gregory VII with particular vigor, including inciting lay riots against married priests.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Building on a long-standing admiration for celibacy dating from at least the fifth century, formalized by decrees such as the 1046 rule that a clerk's son cannot be a bishop.
examples: Gregory VII's calls on the laity not to attend mass celebrated by a married ('recalcitrant') priest
Bishops' appeal to Saint Paul's requirement that a bishop be 'the husband of one wife,' against the stricter reforming interpretation
objections: The married secular clergy's own objection, especially strong in Germany, which contributed to clerical support for the Emperor against Gregory VII
competing_positions: The Eastern Church's continued practice of allowing married parish priests
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly tied to preventing hereditary transmission of Church property and to reinforcing clerical separateness and authority.

core_concepts.name: The Investiture Controversy and the conflict of Gregory VII and Henry IV
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Bishops were traditionally invested with the ring and staff symbolizing their office by their feudal overlord (Emperor or king). Gregory VII insisted these symbols be given by the Pope instead, as part of detaching the ecclesiastical from the feudal hierarchy. The resulting conflict escalated to mutual depositions and excommunications between Gregory and Henry IV, Henry's penitential submission at Canossa (1077), and ultimately Henry's later military triumph and Gregory's death as a virtual prisoner of the Normans in 1085.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The eleventh- and twelfth-century struggle over whether secular rulers or the Pope had the right to appoint (invest) bishops with the symbols of ecclesiastical office, understood by Russell as part of the broader project of separating Church governance from feudal control.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It was the decisive episode establishing (in the long run) papal supremacy over lay control of Church appointments, even though its immediate outcome (Gregory's death in exile) looked like defeat.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Began over the 1075 dispute concerning the archbishopric of Milan, escalating through mutual excommunication and deposition between Gregory VII and Henry IV.
examples: Henry IV's three days waiting barefoot in penitential garb outside the castle of Canossa (1077) before being received back into communion
Henry's later capture of Rome (1084) with an antipope, and the Normans' brutal sack of Rome in relieving Gregory, who died in their custody in 1085
competing_positions: The Emperor's claim, expressed at the Council of Worms, to be above all earthly (including papal) judgment
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The conflict continued, with more moderation, under Gregory's successors, and its later stages recur throughout Chapters XI and XII.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The central church-state conflict of the medieval period.

arguments.title: The ontological argument for God's existence
premises: God is defined as the greatest possible object of thought.
If an object of thought does not exist, another object exactly like it that does exist would be greater than it.
Therefore, if the greatest possible object of thought did not exist, a greater object (namely, the same one, but existing) would be conceivable.
arguments.conclusion: The greatest possible object of thought -- God -- must exist, since otherwise something greater than 'the greatest possible object of thought' would be possible, which is a contradiction.
arguments.explanation: Russell frames the argument's real philosophical question as: is there anything we can think of which, by the mere fact that we can think of it, is thereby shown to exist outside our thought? If yes, there is a bridge from pure thought to reality; if not, there is not. Russell notes Plato had already used a similar move to argue for the objective reality of ideas, but no one before Anselm had stated the argument in this pure logical form.
objections: The argument was criticized at the time and largely forgotten until the thirteenth century
Thomas Aquinas rejected it, holding that we do not know God's essence well enough to derive His existence from it, and his rejection has generally prevailed among Catholic theologians
Kant is credited with having 'demolished it once for all'
implications: Established a durable, recurring philosophical problem (whether existence can be derived from a concept) that reappears in Descartes, Leibniz, Hegel, and Bradley

arguments.title: God's power to act contrary to the law of contradiction
premises: Omnipotence, taken without qualification, implies the power to do absolutely anything, including things that violate the law of contradiction.
Undoing the past is an example of something ordinarily thought logically impossible.
arguments.conclusion: God can do things contrary to the law of contradiction, and can undo the past.
arguments.explanation: Russell notes this view was later rejected by Saint Thomas and has, since Aquinas's time, been considered unorthodox -- illustrating a genuine and consequential disagreement within Christian philosophy about the scope of divine omnipotence.
objections: Rejected by Thomas Aquinas, whose authority has made the contrary view (that God cannot make a contradiction true, e.g. cannot make a man be an ass) the settled orthodox position, as covered in the chapter on Aquinas
implications: Raises the general question, recurring throughout medieval philosophy, of whether logical necessity itself binds God or is instead simply God's free creation

key_distinctions: Simony (buying/selling ecclesiastical office) vs. legitimate appointment on grounds of merit
Clerical celibacy as ascetic ideal vs. the practical, property-related motives for enforcing it
Investiture by secular ruler vs. investiture by the Pope

Reason as subordinate to faith (Anselm's later position, 'I believe in order to understand') vs. reason as an independent or superior authority (as with the Berengar-John the Scot line and, before them, John the Scot himself)
The Platonic tradition in early scholasticism (Anselm) vs. the Aristotelian tradition that would come to dominate with Roscelin and his successors
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Anselm's philosophy is explicitly derived mainly from Saint Augustine, from whom he acquires Platonic elements (including a proof of God's existence from the reality of Platonic ideas, and an argument for the Trinity via Neoplatonic reasoning reminiscent of Plotinus). Berengar of Tours's appeal to reason's superiority over authority explicitly invokes John the Scot (Chapter VIII), leading to John's posthumous condemnation as well.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Anselm's ontological argument becomes a recurring touchstone across the history of philosophy: rejected by Aquinas (Chapter XIII), revived by Descartes, developed further by Leibniz, and 'demolished' (in Russell's phrase) by Kant, while still underlying aspects of Hegel's system and Bradley's philosophy. Roscelin, described here only as Anselm's younger contemporary, is explicitly flagged as the true beginning of the properly 'scholastic' (Aristotelian) tradition, to be treated in the next chapter [note: covered in Chapter XI in this edition's numbering].
political_social_context: The chapter narrates the eleventh-century struggle for power between reforming clergy and both feudal lay authorities and the Roman aristocracy: the Emperor's initial sponsorship of papal reform (Henry III deposing corrupt popes and installing Leo IX and others), the 1059 papal election decree removing the Emperor from the process, the Patarine popular reform movement in Milan (allied with the papacy against the local, aristocracy-linked archbishop), and the full-scale Investiture Controversy between Gregory VII and Henry IV, including the dramatic penance at Canossa and Gregory's eventual death in exile.
religion_science_culture_context: Surveys the network of new monastic orders founded in this reforming spirit: Cluny (910, William the Pious), the Camaldolese (1012, Romuald), the Carthusians (1084, Bruno of Cologne), and the Cistercians (1098, joined by Saint Bernard in 1113, noted for its austere rejection of stained glass and use of lay brethren). Also treats the beginnings of scholastic philosophy as growing directly out of this same reform-minded monastic culture, and the doctrine of transubstantiation, which became formal Church dogma only in 1079 though long generally believed.
russell_presentation: Russell gives the reform movement a double reading: he takes seriously its genuine moral motivation (disgust at simony and clerical immorality) while insisting, just as strongly, on an underlying, initially unconscious but increasingly open power motive -- the separation and elevation of clergy as a caste, which made an eventual, structurally inevitable conflict with the Emperor. He treats the campaign against clerical marriage with a certain dry skepticism, noting that reformers habitually called married priests' wives 'concubines' when 'marriage' would have been more accurate, and stressing the property-related, non-doctrinal motives behind enforced celibacy. On Gregory VII, Russell is respectful of the sincerity of his self-conception (as the mouthpiece of Saint Peter, entitled to depose an immoral Emperor) while noting drily that 'on a mundane calculation' this self-confidence 'was not justified,' and that Gregory's apparent triumph at Canossa was in fact 'illusory' -- he had, in Russell's phrase, been 'caught out by the rules of his own theology.' On Anselm's ontological argument, Russell is notably even-handed and philosophically engaged for a work of history, treating it as a serious and historically influential piece of reasoning worth respect 'whether valid or not,' rather than dismissing it as a medieval curiosity.
key_takeaways: Eleventh-century Church reform combined genuine moral concern (over simony and clerical immorality) with an increasingly explicit political goal: separating the clergy from lay control and increasing clerical power, which made conflict with the Emperor structurally inevitable.

Simony (the sale of ecclesiastical office) and clerical marriage ('concubinage') were the two chief targets of reform, both attacked on moral grounds but also because they tied the Church to secular and hereditary interests.
Nicholas II's 1059 decree removed the Emperor from papal elections, assigning the choice to the cardinal bishops -- a crucial step in papal independence from lay control.

Gregory VII's Investiture Controversy with Henry IV culminated in Henry's penitential submission at Canossa (1077), but this victory proved illusory, and Gregory died in 1085 as a virtual prisoner of the Normans after Henry's later military successes.

Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, devised the 'ontological argument' for God's existence -- deriving God's existence from the very definition of God as the greatest conceivable being -- a proof rejected by Aquinas and Kant but revived by Descartes and Leibniz and still philosophically influential.

The century's new reforming monastic orders (Cluny, Camaldolese, Carthusians, Cistercians) provided the institutional and personal foundation for both ecclesiastical reform and the first stirrings of scholastic philosophy.
study_notes:
Treat this chapter as having two intertwined stories: an institutional one (how the Church disciplined itself and won independence from lay control) and a philosophical one (the first genuinely new argument in medieval Western thought, Anselm's ontological argument). The institutional story is worth reading skeptically in the way Russell himself reads it: notice how consistently a stated moral motive (holiness, celibacy, freedom from corruption) turns out to be inseparable from a material or political one (property, appointments, revenue, independence from kings). This is a pattern you should watch for again in later chapters (e.g. the campaigns against heresy, or the mendicant orders' vow of poverty).

On Anselm's argument, resist the temptation to dismiss it too quickly as merely a medieval curiosity: Russell insists it deserves serious treatment because of its distinguished later history (Descartes, Leibniz, Kant, Hegel, Bradley) and because it isolates, in unusually pure form, a real philosophical question -- can existence ever be derived from a mere concept? Keep this question in mind as a thread to follow into later chapters, where Aquinas will reject the argument on the grounds that we do not, in fact, know God's essence well enough to reason from it.

glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The purchase or sale of ecclesiastical office, sacraments, or preferment, condemned by eleventh-century reformers as both sinful and structurally corrupting (tying appointment to wealth and to secular patronage rather than merit).

glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The ceremonial conferral of the ring and staff symbolizing episcopal office, historically performed by the bishop's feudal overlord; Gregory VII's insistence that only the Pope could invest bishops triggered the Investiture Controversy with Henry IV.
related_concepts: The Investiture Controversy and the conflict of Gregory VII and Henry IV

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: An argument that tries to prove God exists just by carefully thinking about what 'God' means, without needing any evidence from the world.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Saint Anselm's a priori argument that God, defined as the greatest possible object of thought, must exist, since a merely conceived but non-existent being would be surpassed in greatness by an otherwise identical being that does exist.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The castle where Emperor Henry IV waited barefoot for three days in the snow to beg Pope Gregory VII's forgiveness in 1077.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The site of Henry IV's 1077 penitential submission to Gregory VII during the Investiture Controversy; though it appeared a papal triumph, Russell notes the victory proved illusory once Gregory discovered Henry's repentance was insincere.
related_concepts: The Investiture Controversy and the conflict of Gregory VII and Henry IV

questions.prompt: What two motives, according to Russell, drove the eleventh-century reform movement, and how did they relate to each other?
questions.answer: An initial, sincere moral motive (correcting corrupt and immoral clergy) and a gradually more explicit political motive (completing the separation of clergy from laity in order to increase clerical power). The moral motive provided the movement's justification, but the political motive made an eventual conflict between Church and Empire structurally inevitable.
questions.explanation: Russell treats these as inseparable throughout the chapter, most explicitly in the campaigns against simony and clerical marriage.

questions.prompt: State Anselm's ontological argument for the existence of God in your own words.
questions.answer: God is defined as the greatest possible object of thought. If such an object did not exist, we could conceive of another, identical object that does exist, and that object would be greater (since existing is greater than merely being conceived). Therefore the greatest possible object of thought must exist, since otherwise a greater one would be conceivable -- a contradiction. Hence God exists.
questions.explanation: This is the first purely a priori proof of God's existence in Western philosophy.

questions.prompt: Who invented the 'ontological argument' for the existence of God, and what position did he hold in the Church?
questions.explanation: Anselm was also a monk at Bec in Normandy before his archbishopric, following the principles of Gregory VII.

questions.prompt: What decree did Pope Nicholas II secure in 1059 concerning papal elections, and why was it significant?
questions.answer: It provided that popes would be chosen first by the cardinal bishops, then by the other cardinals, and last (purely formally) by the clergy and people of Rome, with no role allotted to the Emperor. It was an essential step in emancipating the papacy from lay (imperial) control.
questions.explanation: This decree removed the Emperor from the papal selection process for the first time.

questions.prompt: Describe the events at Canossa in 1077 and explain why Russell calls Gregory VII's apparent victory there 'illusory.'
questions.answer: Emperor Henry IV, having been excommunicated, crossed the Alps in winter and waited barefoot for three days outside the castle of Canossa in penitential garb before being absolved by Gregory VII. Russell calls the victory illusory because Gregory, bound by his own theology to accept a penitent's repentance, wrongly believed Henry's contrition was sincere; Henry in fact used the reprieve to regain strength, and ultimately defeated Gregory's allies, forcing Gregory into exile, where he died in 1085.
questions.explanation: This shows how a symbolic religious triumph did not translate into lasting political victory.

questions.prompt: Compare Peter Damian's view of divine omnipotence with the position later taken by Thomas Aquinas.
questions.answer: Peter Damian argued in On Divine Omnipotence that God can act contrary to the law of contradiction, including undoing the past. Thomas Aquinas later rejected this view, holding that God cannot make a contradiction true (for instance, cannot make a man be an ass); Aquinas's position has been the orthodox one ever since.
questions.explanation: This marks a genuine substantive disagreement within Christian philosophy about the scope of divine power.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the objections to simony that made it more than merely a private sin, according to Russell's account of the reformers' reasoning.
questions.answer: Premise: simony causes ecclesiastical preferment to be distributed by wealth rather than merit. Premise: it confirms lay (royal or noble) authority over the appointment of bishops, tying the episcopate to secular power. Premise: it assimilates bishoprics into the feudal system of purchased offices. Premise: a man who has purchased his office is naturally anxious to recoup the cost, encouraging worldly rather than spiritual conduct. Conclusion: simony was not merely sinful but structurally undermined clerical independence and spiritual seriousness, making its suppression a necessary part of the wider reform campaign.
questions.explanation: This argument shows why simony, not just clerical marriage, was central to the reformers' broader project of clerical independence from lay control.

questions.prompt: Who denied transubstantiation in the eleventh century, and who wrote against him?
questions.answer: Berengar of Tours denied transubstantiation and was twice compelled to recant; his heresies were combated by Lanfranc in his book De corpore et sanguine Domini.
questions.explanation: Berengar's rationalism (appealing to John the Scot's authority for the superiority of reason) also led to John the Scot's own posthumous condemnation.
